concept.name: Model risk
concept.definition: The potential for adverse consequences — financial loss, poor business decisions, reputational damage — from decisions based on model outputs that are incorrect or misused. Per Federal Reserve SR 11-7, model risk arises primarily when a model has fundamental errors or when it is used incorrectly or without regard for its limitations and assumptions.
concept.intuition: Every model is a simplified map of reality; model risk is what happens when you drive off the edge of the map while trusting it.
concept.mechanics: Managed through a model risk management framework: sound development and documentation, independent validation (conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring, outcomes analysis such as back-testing), 'effective challenge' by informed parties, model inventories, and senior-management governance. Risk grows with model complexity, input uncertainty, breadth of use, and potential impact.
concept.formula: No single-quantity formula; SR 11-7 frames the sources as (1) fundamental model error and (2) incorrect or inappropriate use.
concept.failure_modes: Validation lags usage: models calibrated in benign regimes get trusted in stressed ones, and back-tests share the model's own assumptions. Widely used models create systemic crowding, with everyone de-risking on the same signal and amplifying the event the model failed to foresee.
concept.misconceptions: Passing validation does not make a model 'true': SR 11-7 stresses that all models are imperfect representations requiring conservative adjustments and informed use, and a precise-looking output is not an accurate one.
concept.example: A VaR model assuming normal returns understates tail losses in a crash; positions sized off its output suffer losses far beyond the reported number — the classic model-risk failure SR 11-7 warns about.

citations.source: Federal Reserve / OCC / FDIC: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 26-2)
